# Issuing, serving, pleading and responding {#sec-dr-commencing}

> *Assessment objective 4: commencing, responding to or progressing a claim.*

## Issuing the claim form

Proceedings are **started** when the court **issues** a claim form at the claimant's request (CPR 7.2)
— but for limitation purposes the claim is **brought** when the claim form is **received** by the court
office. Both propositions matter, and they answer different questions.

The **Part 7** procedure is the standard route for a disputed claim. **Part 8** is for claims where
there is unlikely to be a substantial dispute of fact, and where the rules require or permit it.

### The claim form (N1)

CPR 16.2 requires the claim form to:

- **name the parties** correctly;
- contain a **concise statement of the nature of the claim**;
- **specify the remedy** sought — though the court may grant a remedy the claimant has not asked for;
- where money is claimed, contain a **statement of value** (CPR 16.3): the amount claimed, or a
  statement that the claimant expects to recover not more than £10,000, more than £10,000 but not more
  than £25,000, more than £25,000 but not more than £100,000, or more than £100,000 — and, if issued
  in the High Court, why the claimant is entitled to issue there;
- be verified by a **statement of truth**.

The **court fee** is calculated on the value claimed, so pleading the claim too high is expensive and
pleading it too low caps recovery.

### Naming the parties

| Defendant | Named as |
|---|---|
| Individual | Full name, with title |
| Sole trader | "*Name* trading as *Business Name*" |
| Partnership | The firm name, where the partners carried on business under it when the cause of action accrued |
| Company | The full registered name, including "Limited" or "plc" |
| LLP | The full registered name |
| Child or protected party | By or through a **litigation friend** |
| Estate | The personal representatives, or if none, an order appointing a person to represent the estate |

### Adding, removing and substituting parties

**CPR 19.2**: the court may **remove**, **add** or **substitute** a party where it is desirable so that
the court can resolve all matters in dispute, or where there is an issue between an existing party and
the new party which it is desirable to resolve.

**CPR 19.4**: the court's **permission** is required to add or substitute a party **after** the claim
form has been served. Before service, the claimant may amend as of right.

**CPR 19.6 — after limitation has expired.** This is the restrictive rule, and it is examined. The
court may add or substitute a party **only if**:

- the relevant limitation period **was current when the proceedings were started**; **and**
- the addition or substitution is **necessary**.

It is "necessary" **only** if the court is satisfied that:

(a) the new party is to be **substituted for a party who was named in the claim form by mistake** for
the new party;
(b) the claim **cannot properly be carried on** by or against the original party unless the new party
is added or substituted; or
(c) the original party has **died** or had a **bankruptcy order** made against them and their interest
or liability has passed to the new party.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
The mistake limb in CPR 19.6(3)(a) covers a mistake **as to name**, not a change of mind about **who to
sue**. Naming "ABC Trading Ltd" when the contracting party was "ABC Trading (Northern) Ltd" is a
mistake. Deciding, after limitation has expired, that you should have sued the director personally as
well as the company is not — that is a new claim against a new party, and CPR 19.6 will not permit it.
:::

## Serving the claim form

### The time limit

**CPR 7.5**: the claimant must complete the **step required** by **12.00 midnight on the calendar day
four months after the date of issue** of the claim form. Where the claim form is to be served **out of
the jurisdiction**, the period is **six months** (CPR 7.5(2)).

The "step required" depends on the method:

| Method | Step required |
|---|---|
| First class post, DX or other next business day delivery | **Posting**, leaving with, delivering to or collection by the relevant service provider |
| Delivery to or leaving at a permitted address | **Delivering** to or leaving the document at the relevant place |
| Personal service under CPR 6.5 | **Leaving** it with the individual |
| Electronic method | **Sending** the email or other transmission |

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Under CPR 7.5 the claimant must complete the **step**, not achieve service, within four months. Posting
the claim form by first class post on the last day is compliant even though deemed service falls
afterwards. This is the single most frequently misunderstood rule in the service topic.
:::

### Extending time for service

**CPR 7.6.** An application to extend must generally be made **within** the period for service. If made
**after** it has expired, the court may only extend if:

- the court has **failed to serve** the claim form; or
- the claimant has taken **all reasonable steps** to comply with CPR 7.5 but has been unable to do so;
  **and**
- in either case, the claimant has acted **promptly** in making the application.

This is deliberately severe, because an extension after limitation has expired deprives the defendant
of an accrued limitation defence.

### The methods and the address

**CPR 6.3** — permitted methods: personal service; first class post, DX or other next business day
delivery service; leaving it at a specified place; fax or other means of **electronic communication**;
or any method authorised by the court.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
Service by **email** is valid only where the party to be served, or their solicitor, has **indicated in
writing** that they are willing to accept service by that means and given an address for it. In *Barton
v Wright Hassall LLP* [2018] UKSC 12 a litigant in person emailed the claim form to the defendant's
solicitors on the last day, without having established their willingness to accept email service. The
Supreme Court refused to validate it retrospectively under CPR 6.15(2), and the claim was lost.
:::

**Who to serve** (CPR 6.7): if the defendant has given in writing the business address of a solicitor
authorised to accept service, the claim form **must** be served on that solicitor. Otherwise CPR 6.9
supplies the place:

| Defendant | Place of service |
|---|---|
| Individual | Usual or last known **residence** |
| Individual being sued in the name of a business | Usual or last known residence, or the **principal or last known place of business** |
| Partnership sued in the firm name | Usual or last known residence of a partner, or the **principal or last known place of business** of the partnership |
| **Company** registered in England and Wales | The **principal office**, or any place of business having a **real connection** with the claim |

A company may alternatively be served at its **registered office** under s.1139 Companies Act 2006.

### Deemed service

**CPR 6.14 — the claim form.** A claim form served within the United Kingdom is deemed to be served on
the **second business day after completion of the relevant step** under CPR 7.5(1). There is a single
rule and no method-by-method table, whatever the actual date of delivery.

**CPR 6.26 — every other document.** Here there *is* a table:

| Method | Deemed date of service |
|---|---|
| First class post, DX or other next business day delivery | The **second day** after posting, if that is a business day; otherwise the **next business day** after that day |
| Delivering to or leaving at a permitted address | If before **4.30 p.m. on a business day**, that day; otherwise the **next business day** |
| Personal service | Same rule as above |
| Fax | Same rule as above |
| Other electronic method | Same rule as above |

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example"}
A claim form is issued on Monday 4 May. The claimant posts it by first class post on Friday 28 August.

**Is service in time?** The four-month period expires at midnight on 4 September. The **step required**
for postal service is **posting**, which happened on 28 August. Service is in time.

**When is it deemed served?** CPR 6.14: the **second business day** after completion of the step.
Posting was Friday; the first business day after is Monday 31 August, the second is Tuesday 1
September. Deemed service is **Tuesday 1 September**, whatever day it actually arrived.

**When is the defence due?** Fourteen days from service of the **particulars of claim**. If the
particulars were served with the claim form, an acknowledgment of service or defence is due by 15
September; filing an acknowledgment extends the defence to 29 September.
:::

### Service by an alternative method

**CPR 6.15.** Where there is a **good reason**, the court may authorise service by a method or at a
place not otherwise permitted. Under **CPR 6.15(2)** it may also, on the same test, order that steps
already taken to bring the claim form to the defendant's attention are to be treated as good service.
The order must specify the method, the **deemed date of service**, and the period for responding.

### Service out of the jurisdiction

Two routes, and the distinction decides the question:

**Without permission** (CPR 6.32–6.33). Available where the English court has power to determine the
claim under the Civil Jurisdiction and Judgments Act 1982, where the contract contains a term to the
effect that the **English court shall have jurisdiction**, or under the Hague 2005 Convention.

**With permission** (CPR 6.36). The claimant must satisfy the **three requirements** set out in
@sec-dr-preaction: a good arguable case within a **PD 6B gateway**, a **serious issue to be tried**, and
that **England is the proper place**. The application is made without notice, supported by evidence, and
the claimant owes a duty of **full and frank disclosure**.

**Mechanics abroad.** Service may be effected through the **foreign government or judicial authority**
or the British consular authority (CPR 6.42), through a **Hague Service Convention** channel where the
destination state is a party, or by any method **permitted by the law of the country** in which service
is to be effected (CPR 6.40(3)) — but **never** by a method that is contrary to that country's law.
The period for responding is extended by PD 6B according to the destination.

## Statements of case

### Particulars of claim

**CPR 16.4**: a **concise statement of the facts** on which the claimant relies; a claim for **interest**
if any, with the basis and, for a specified sum, the percentage rate, the dates from and to which it is
claimed and the daily rate; any claim for **aggravated or exemplary damages** or **provisional damages**;
and a **statement of truth**.

The particulars must be served with the claim form or **within 14 days** after service of the claim
form (CPR 7.4), and in any event within the four-month period for serving the claim form.

The content follows the cause of action:

| Contract claim | Tort (negligence) claim |
|---|---|
| The status of the parties | The status of the parties |
| The **contract**: date, parties, whether written or oral, consideration | The facts giving rise to a **duty of care** |
| The **terms** relied on, express or implied | The **duty** owed |
| **Performance** by the claimant | The acts or omissions constituting **breach** |
| The **breach**, with particulars | **Causation** |
| **Causation** and **loss**, with a schedule of loss | The **damage**, with a schedule of loss |
| Interest | Interest |

### Defence

**CPR 16.5** requires the defendant to state, in relation to **each allegation**, whether it is:

- **denied** — and if so, the defendant must state the **reasons** for the denial and, if putting
  forward a different version of events, state that version;
- **admitted**; or
- **neither admitted nor denied**, because the defendant is unable to admit or deny it and requires the
  claimant to prove it.

**Failure to deal with an allegation is a deemed admission** — except that a defendant who fails to deal
with an allegation but has set out the nature of their case in relation to the issue is taken to
require it to be proved, and a defendant who fails to deal with an allegation about the **amount of
money claimed** is taken to require it to be proved. The defence must dispute the claimant's statement
of value if the defendant disputes it, and must give its own.

The defence must also plead any **positive case** and any **limitation** defence, and must be verified
by a statement of truth.

### Reply, Part 20 claims and further information

**Reply** (CPR 16.7). Optional. A claimant who does not file one is not taken to admit the matters
raised in the defence. A reply is needed to answer a positive case in the defence that the particulars
of claim do not already address.

**Additional claims under Part 20:**

| Claim | Permission needed? |
|---|---|
| **Counterclaim against the claimant** | **No**, if filed with the defence; otherwise yes (CPR 20.4) |
| Counterclaim against a person **other than** the claimant | **Yes** (CPR 20.5) |
| Claim for **contribution or indemnity against a co-defendant** | **No**, if filed with the defence, or within 28 days of a party being added (CPR 20.6) |
| Any **other additional claim** — for example against a third party | **No**, if issued **before or at the same time as** the defence is filed; otherwise **yes** (CPR 20.7) |

An additional claim is treated as a claim in its own right, and Part 20 applies the ordinary rules to
it with modifications.

**Further information** (CPR 18). A party may serve a **written request** for clarification of any matter
in dispute or additional information about it, giving a date for response. If the other party does not
comply, an **application** may be made. The request must be **concise and strictly confined** to what is
reasonably necessary and proportionate.

### Amendments

**CPR 17.1**: a party may amend a statement of case **at any time before it has been served** on any
other party. After service, amendment requires the **written consent of all the other parties** or the
**permission of the court**.

**CPR 17.4 — amendment after limitation has expired.** Where the relevant limitation period was current
when the proceedings started, the court may allow an amendment only:

- to add or substitute a **new claim** arising out of **the same facts or substantially the same facts**
  as a claim already made; or
- to correct a **mistake as to the name of a party**, where the mistake was **genuine** and not one
  which would cause reasonable doubt as to the identity of the party; or
- to **alter the capacity** in which a party claims.

The court will also consider whether the amendment is in accordance with the overriding objective —
lateness, the effect on the trial date and the costs consequences all bear on the discretion.

### The statement of truth

Every statement of case must be verified by a statement of truth. Since April 2020 the prescribed
wording is:

> I believe that the facts stated in this [document] are true. I understand that proceedings for
> contempt of court may be brought against anyone who makes, or causes to be made, a false statement in
> a document verified by a statement of truth without an honest belief in its truth.

It may be signed by the party, by a person with authority (for a company, a person holding a senior
position, who must state which), or by the party's legal representative — who signs on the party's
behalf and must have the party's authority and have explained the consequences.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
A solicitor may sign a statement of truth on the client's behalf, but may **never** verify a statement
the solicitor knows or believes to be false. Where the client insists on advancing an account the
solicitor knows to be untrue, the solicitor must not draft or sign it, and will usually have to **cease
to act** — without disclosing the reason, because the reason is confidential.
:::

## Responding to a claim

### The time limits

| Step | Time limit |
|---|---|
| **Acknowledgment of service** | **14 days** after service of the particulars of claim (CPR 10.3) |
| **Defence**, where no acknowledgment filed | **14 days** after service of the particulars of claim (CPR 15.4) |
| **Defence**, where an acknowledgment has been filed | **28 days** after service of the particulars of claim |
| **Agreed extension** of the defence | Up to a further **28 days**, by agreement, notifying the court in writing (CPR 15.5) — so a maximum of **56 days** without a court order |
| **Application disputing jurisdiction** | **14 days** after filing the acknowledgment of service (CPR 11) |

### The options

**Admit** (Part 14). The defendant may admit the whole or part of the claim. For a **specified** sum,
the claimant may then obtain judgment; the defendant may ask for time to pay, and the rate of payment
is determined by the court or by agreement.

**Defend.** File an acknowledgment of service and/or a defence, and consider a counterclaim.

**Dispute the court's jurisdiction** (Part 11). The defendant must **first file an acknowledgment of
service** — filing one is not a submission to the jurisdiction — and then apply **within 14 days**. If
the defendant files a **defence** without applying, they are **treated as having accepted** that the
court has jurisdiction.

**Do nothing** — and face default judgment.

::: {.callout-important title="Exam trap"}
To challenge jurisdiction, the defendant must **acknowledge service and then apply within 14 days**.
Doing nothing loses the point (default judgment follows) and filing a defence loses it too (submission).
The acknowledgment of service form has a tick box for "I intend to contest jurisdiction" precisely for
this purpose.
:::

### Default judgment

**Part 12.** The claimant may obtain judgment in default where the defendant has failed to file an
acknowledgment of service **or** a defence, and the time for doing so has expired. It is entered
administratively on request for a specified sum, and on application otherwise.

Default judgment is **not** available where:

- the claim is under **Part 8**;
- the defendant has applied for **summary judgment** or to have the claim **struck out**, and the
  application has not been disposed of;
- the defendant has **satisfied** the claim; or
- the defendant has **admitted** the claim and applied for time to pay.

**Setting aside** (Part 13):

- **CPR 13.2 — mandatory.** The court **must** set the judgment aside if it was **wrongly entered** —
  because the time for responding had not in fact expired, or the claim had been satisfied, or the
  defendant had filed an acknowledgment or defence in time.
- **CPR 13.3 — discretionary.** The court **may** set it aside if the defendant has a **real prospect
  of successfully defending** the claim, or if it appears to the court that there is **some other good
  reason** why the judgment should be set aside or the defendant should be allowed to defend. On any
  such application the court **must have regard to whether the application was made promptly**.

::: {.callout-tip title="Worked example"}
Particulars of claim are deemed served on 1 October. The defendant, who has been abroad, files nothing.
On 20 October the claimant enters default judgment. The defendant returns on 5 November, and applies to
set the judgment aside on 20 December, saying the goods were defective.

**Was the judgment properly entered?** The defence was due by 15 October and nothing was filed, so yes.
CPR 13.2 does not apply.

**Will it be set aside?** Only under CPR 13.3, and the defendant must show a real prospect of
successfully defending — a defective goods defence may well qualify. But the court **must have regard
to promptness**, and a six-week delay after returning is a serious obstacle. On these facts the
application may fail on delay alone, and if it succeeds the defendant will almost certainly bear the
costs thrown away.
:::

### Discontinuance and settlement

**Discontinuance** (Part 38). The claimant may discontinue at any time by filing and serving a **notice
of discontinuance**. Permission is required where the court has granted an **interim injunction** or
where any party has given an **undertaking** to the court, or where the claimant has received an
**interim payment**. Where there is more than one claimant, the consent of the others or the court's
permission is needed. Unless the court orders otherwise, the claimant is **liable for the defendant's
costs** to the date of discontinuance (CPR 38.6).

**Settlement** may be recorded by:

- a **consent order**, where the terms are to be enforceable as an order of the court and there is
  nothing confidential;
- a **Tomlin order** — an order **staying** the proceedings on agreed terms set out in a **schedule**,
  with permission to apply for the purpose of carrying those terms into effect. The schedule is not
  part of the order and need not be a matter of public record, which is why it is used where the terms
  are confidential or go beyond what the court could order;
- acceptance of a **Part 36 offer**, which stays the claim automatically; or
- a simple **settlement agreement**, with the claim then discontinued.

## Check yourself

**Q1.** A claim form is issued on 3 March. On 30 June the claimant's solicitor posts it to the
defendant's solicitors, who are authorised in writing to accept service, by first class post. It
arrives on 2 July.

Which of the following is correct?

A. Service is out of time, because the claim form was not received by the defendant's solicitors within
four months of issue.

B. Service is in time: the step required for postal service is posting, which was completed on 30 June,
within four months of issue; the claim form is deemed served on the second business day after posting.

C. Service is in time, and the claim form is deemed served on the day it arrived, 2 July.

D. Service is out of time, because service on solicitors is not permitted.

E. Service is in time, and the claim form is deemed served on the day it was posted, 30 June.

**Q2.** Particulars of claim are deemed served on a defendant on Tuesday 6 October. The defendant files
an acknowledgment of service on 15 October, indicating an intention to defend.

By when must the defence be filed, assuming no agreement or order extending time?

A. 20 October, being 14 days after the acknowledgment of service.

B. 20 October, being 14 days after service of the particulars of claim.

C. 3 November, being 28 days after service of the particulars of claim.

D. 12 November, being 28 days after the acknowledgment of service.

E. 1 December, being 56 days after service of the particulars of claim.

**Q3.** A claimant sued "Northgate Logistics Limited". The contracting party was in fact "Northgate
Logistics (UK) Limited", a different company in the same group with a similar name. The limitation
period expired two months after the claim form was issued. The claimant now applies to substitute the
correct company.

Which of the following is correct?

A. The application must be refused, because the limitation period has expired.

B. The application may be granted under CPR 19.6 if the limitation period was current when the
proceedings were started and the substitution is necessary — which it is where the new party is being
substituted for a party named in the claim form by mistake for the new party.

C. The application may be granted as of right, because the claim form has not yet been amended.

D. The application must be refused, because the claimant chose to sue a different legal person and that
is not a mistake as to name.

E. The claimant must issue fresh proceedings and rely on s.33 of the Limitation Act 1980.

**Q4.** A defendant based in Germany is served with an English claim form. The defendant believes the
English court has no jurisdiction because the contract contains an exclusive German jurisdiction clause.

What must the defendant do to preserve the point?

A. File a defence setting out the jurisdiction objection.

B. Write to the court explaining that it does not accept jurisdiction, and take no further step.

C. File an acknowledgment of service indicating an intention to contest jurisdiction, and apply under
Part 11 within 14 days after filing it.

D. Apply for summary judgment under Part 24.

E. Ignore the proceedings, because a foreign defendant cannot be bound by an English judgment.

**Q5.** A defendant, having filed a defence, wishes to bring a claim for an indemnity against a
sub-contractor who is not a party to the proceedings. The defence was filed three weeks ago.

Which of the following is correct?

A. The defendant may issue the additional claim without permission at any time.

B. The defendant requires the court's permission, because the additional claim was not issued before or
at the same time as the defence was filed.

C. The defendant may only bring the claim in separate proceedings.

D. The defendant requires the consent of the claimant.

E. The defendant may issue the additional claim without permission because it is a claim for an
indemnity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answers and explanations"}

**Q1 — B.** CPR 7.5(1): the claimant must complete the **step required** within four months of issue,
and for first class post that step is **posting**. Posting on 30 June, from a claim form issued on 3
March, is within four months. Deemed service under CPR 6.14 is the **second business day** after
completion of the step, regardless of actual delivery.

- **A** and **D** apply the wrong test: what matters is the step, not receipt, and CPR 6.7 requires
  service on a solicitor authorised in writing to accept it.
- **C** applies the actual date of delivery. CPR 6.14 is a deeming provision and the real date is
  irrelevant.
- **E** deems service on the day of the step, which is what CPR 6.14 expressly does not do.

**Q2 — C.** CPR 15.4(1)(b): where the defendant files an acknowledgment of service, the defence must be
filed **28 days after service of the particulars of claim** — not 28 days after the acknowledgment.
Twenty-eight days from 6 October is 3 November.

- **A** and **D** run time from the acknowledgment, which is the classic error.
- **B** applies the 14-day period that operates only where no acknowledgment is filed.
- **E** applies the maximum available **with** an agreed extension under CPR 15.5, which the facts
  exclude.

**Q3 — B.** CPR 19.6. The limitation period was current when the proceedings were started, and
substitution is "necessary" under CPR 19.6(3)(a) where the new party is to be substituted for a party
named in the claim form **by mistake** for the new party. Suing the wrong company in a group because of
a similar name is a classic mistake as to identity of this kind, provided the mistake was genuine and
would not cause reasonable doubt as to who was intended.

- **A** treats the expiry of limitation as an absolute bar, which CPR 19.6 exists to qualify.
- **C** ignores the need for permission after service and the special rule after limitation.
- **D** is the strongest distractor, and would be right if the claimant had deliberately sued one legal
  person and later changed its mind. Here the intention was always to sue the contracting party.
- **E** applies s.33, which is available only in personal injury and fatal accident claims.

**Q4 — C.** CPR Part 11. The defendant must file an **acknowledgment of service** — which is not a
submission to the jurisdiction — and then apply for an order declaring that the court has no
jurisdiction, or should not exercise it, **within 14 days** after filing the acknowledgment.

- **A** is fatal: filing a defence without making the application means the defendant is **treated as
  having accepted** that the court has jurisdiction.
- **B** and **E** invite default judgment.
- **D** attacks the merits, not the forum, and engaging with the merits risks submission.

**Q5 — B.** CPR 20.7(3): an additional claim other than a counterclaim against the claimant or a claim
for contribution or indemnity **against an existing co-defendant** may be made without permission only
if it is issued **before or at the same time as** the defendant files their defence. The defence was
filed three weeks ago, so permission is required.

- **A** and **E** overlook the timing condition. Note the distinction being tested: CPR 20.6 allows a
  contribution or indemnity claim against an **existing co-defendant** without permission if filed with
  the defence; this sub-contractor is **not yet a party**, so CPR 20.7 applies.
- **C** is wrong: Part 20 exists so that related claims can be tried together.
- **D** requires a consent the rules do not call for.

:::
